extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, metallurgists/miners, horticulturists, and practical artisans/readers of the Philosophical Transactions
extracted.subtask_description: Detailed procedural descriptions and practical guidance for tin washing, kiln/blowing-house operation, ore dressing and handling, plus experimental methods and observations for plant sap motion, grafting, transplanting, cider-making, and dyeing; aimed at documenting methods and results for replication or improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trambling / huddle-head technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a long square tie (board) where a trambling man casts up ore about an inch thick on a board (huddle head), then with the shovel cut and divide it longways about half an inch asunder so that a gentle flow of water from an upper plain board carries away the filth and lighter matter first and then the tin falls into the huddle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut the ore longways, maintain gentle water flow from above, and stroke/smooth the surface transversely with the foot to make the surface plainer so heterogeneous matter passes away quicker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate concentrates into forehead, middle, tails and re-process
rubrics_metrics.description: When the huddle is full, separate the collected material into forehead, middle, and tails and re-trample the latter parts to concentrate further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish and re-process the parts successively; the forehead may be re-trambled in a second huddle and its forehead carried to a drawing huddle for further refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of drawing huddle for final washing (black tin)
rubrics_metrics.description: A drawing huddle (plain sloping board without a tie) is used to wash and finish the ore called black tin, making it ready for the blowing-house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the drawing huddle wash once with a trambling shovel to obtain 'black tin' that is completely ready for smelting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sizing via hair sieve as alternative to drawing huddle
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of a drawing huddle, a hair sieve may be used to sift the material; remainder is cast back into the tails for further trambling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sift through a hair sieve, return the retained material to tails, and retramble the ore; use sizing where finer separation is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dilving (canvas-sieve washing) to remove filth
rubrics_metrics.description: Put concentrated forehead material into a canvas sieve holding water and in a large tub shake it so filth runs over the rim leaving black tin behind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After dilving, store black tin in covered and locked hogsheads until the next blowing; 'dilve' by vigorous washing in canvas sieve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management of tails via strakes and size-sorting
rubrics_metrics.description: Tails are cast into strakes (pits) which commonly contain two sorts of tin: too small and too large; the large is reground in a crazemill and then trampled; the small is dressed on a reck with shovel and water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use successive strakes to collect tails, separate by size, regrind the larger pieces in a crazemill (two-stone mill) and dress small fragments on a reck for reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reck (dressing frame) specification and use
rubrics_metrics.description: A reck is a frame about 3.5 feet broad and 6 feet long, mounted on iron pegs so it hangs in equilibrium and can be rocked like a cradle for dressing small tin with shovel and water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct and mount the reck to allow rocking movement for even dressing; use it to wash and make small tin fit for use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tin-kiln (blowing-house) basic construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Tin-kiln described as four-square with a large top moor stone (about six by four feet) with a hole above and another similar stone placed about a foot beneath; an open place at back allows flames to ascend from a strong furze fire beneath; forepart resembles a common oven with chimney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build kiln with top and bottom stones, provision for fuel fire of furze below, holes for feeding ore and airflow, and a chimney at the fore part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burning off 'mundic' (arsenical/impurity) in kiln
rubrics_metrics.description: When mundic (impurity that makes tin brittle) is present, place black tin on top stone of a thoroughly heated kiln, cast it down onto the bottom stone in a layer ~3–4 inches thick, cover the top hole with green turfs, and constantly rake the tin so mundic rises and is burned away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor flame colour: blue flame indicates mundic burning; when flame turns yellow and stench lessens mundic is consumed. Keep raking to expose all parts and thrust material into the open fire behind when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hot ore removal, cooling, quenching and reprocessing
rubrics_metrics.description: When the fire-below area becomes full of tin, coals and ashes, rake the mass out through the square hole near the back and allow to cool in open air (may take ~3 days); if rapid cooling necessary quench with water which makes it like mortar, but always re-tramble or wash before placing into the alman furnace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer natural cooling to preserve texture but quench if time prohibits; always re-dress after cooling before smelting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fuel selection by ore type and stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Moor-tin ( peat/moor-excavated tin) melts best with charked moor-coal; country tin runs best with an equal proportion of charcoal and peat for the first run; remelting slags requires charcoal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose fuel type based on ore origin and process stage: use charked moor-coal for moor-tin, mixed charcoal/peat for initial runs of country tin, and charcoal for remelting slags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of mount-egg (iron-rich slag)
rubrics_metrics.description: A particular slag (mount-egg) in the bottom of the float, tin-coloured but largely iron, can be identified because it is attracted by the pole of a loadstone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test suspect slag with a magnet/loadstone to detect iron-rich mount-egg; treat accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tipping a cut twig to reveal sap (detection method)
rubrics_metrics.description: A separated twig that is dry will show moisture at both ends if the cut end is slightly tipped with a knife, indicating internal vessels and the presence of sap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a small tip or nick at the far end of a separated twig to provoke visible sap exudation for diagnosing internal sap presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ligature experiments to probe vessel behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying tight ligatures (silk thread or other) to branches does not always produce asymmetrical swelling; cutting the bark or shaving round the branch above/below a tie can produce milky juice exuding from many small holes indicating veins are over-thronged rather than simply intercepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ligatures and then surface incisions to observe where and how juice emerges; interpret bleeding above and below ties as evidence about vessel connectivity and pressure rather than mere local turgescence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heating (proximity to fire) as a method to induce bleeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Bringing cut twigs/poles within the warmth/air of a fire often causes them to bleed (exude sap) quickly even when not sensibly warmer, indicating a heat-related trigger for sap motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use controlled warming (not necessarily direct heating) to induce sap flow in experiments; note species differ in responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of orientation and handling on bleeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Holding poles vertically, inverting them, or quickly balancing and inverting can promote or inhibit bleeding: poles held perpendicularly bleed; some separated twigs held with cut end down did not bleed until inverted; repeated heating and manipulation can eventually stop bleeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record orientation and handling carefully during sap experiments; inversion and upright holding can change apparent sap flow and must be controlled for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of bark and surface condition in visible sap exudation
rubrics_metrics.description: Poles entirely bared of bark show no moisture when heated, whereas half-bared poles bleed from those circles under the remaining bark; in some species bared pith may still show internal moisture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve or remove bark deliberately as an experimental variable; recognize that bark presence influences where moisture appears but internal tissues may still hold sap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pith sealing does not prevent sap exudation by heat
rubrics_metrics.description: Sealing one or both ends of the pith with hard wax on a willow pole does not prevent the pole from bleeding under warmth of a fire, implying sap paths outside the pith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seal pith when testing the role of central pith versus peripheral tissues; persistence of bleeding implicates other pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal and weather influences on bleeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Trees and twigs show seasonal differences: some species bleed after hard frosts when weather relaxes; a twig that did not bleed on a very cold morning might do so the next day after frost breaks; birch, maple, sycamore, walnut and willow show differing seasonal bleeding patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan sap experiments across seasons/temperature cycles; note that recent frost history, exposure to wind, and microclimate (e.g., shelter against walls) affect readiness to bleed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pole preparation and water-permeation test
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a vessel at an end of a cut branch with wax rings and pour water in; water will sink into the pores and run through the branch, emerging from the distant end, demonstrating permeability through wood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use waxed end-water tests to demonstrate wood porosity and directional movement; results may vary by species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cider improvement by cask selection
rubrics_metrics.description: To increase richness of cider in taste and colour, use a new cask provided it is made of very well-seasoned timber; otherwise a new cask may spoil the cider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose new casks only if timber is thoroughly seasoned; otherwise prefer older suitable casks to avoid spoilage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grafting compatibility affects fruit and cider quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain graft combinations (example: red streake grafted on gennet moyle stock) produce better fruit and smoother cider; incompatible combinations (crab stocks with fruit not liked by the soil) can lead to canker in graft and stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select rootstock/scion combinations that agree with each other and the soil; monitor for canker and replace or re-graft onto compatible stock where observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Season and method for transplanting trees
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer transplanting later (around Valentine's Day) rather than in October to reduce losses from winter frost; prune in winter to shape the tree in advance; preserve and set roots as large as possible though some practitioners advocate cutting roots short to promote new root growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect newly transplanted trees from frost (cannot fully be protected) and from drought by watering and ground covering; when transplanting aim to keep as much root mass as practical, but recognize this is debated and species-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Root handling trade-off (large root preservation vs short cuts)
rubrics_metrics.description: One practice is to preserve as large a root mass as possible (believed to contain more strength/sap); others say short-cut roots do better because they send forth new roots that draw sap best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider species and local experience: preserve roots for immediate vigor, but consider short-root practice for species that readily produce new roots (observe outcomes and adapt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of salts and reagents to alter and fix vegetable/flower colours
rubrics_metrics.description: Acid salts tend to advance and deepen red colours in flowers/berries; urinous salts and alkalies change reds/blues/whites to green and then to yellow, or otherwise alter hues; specific sequences (e.g., lye then oil of vitriol) can produce and fix purple from certain materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply reagents intentionally: acids (e.g., oil of vitriol) can make cochineal vividly crimson; alkalies/urinous spirits transform and can advance colours of leaves/wood. Test small samples and record reagent sequence for reproducible dyeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific dyeing sequences (glastum and fungus examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Blue seed husks of glastum sylvestre when diluted stain blue; affusion of lye (alkali) changes that blue to green; touching the green/blue with oil of vitriol (acid) dyes a purple—these three colours will stand. Tops of fungus tubulosus with red knots, upon affusion of lye, will strike a purple and stand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stepwise reagent treatment (alkali then acid) on particular plant materials to produce multiple stable colours; record drying and fixation outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cochineal treatment rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Cochineal (naturally red) upon affusion of oil of vitriol (acid salt) gives the most vivid crimson; with urinous salts and alkalies it changes to an obscure colour between violet and purple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use acid treatment to produce vivid crimson from cochineal; apply alkalies when seeking violet/purple shades, recognizing reversibility and hue shifts.
